analysis.one_liner: Creates federal patient protections for HMO and managed care plans, including emergency coverage, specialist access, and appeals rights.
analysis.headline: A managed-care patient protection bill with 240 cosponsors — a majority of the House — never got a vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set federal rules for health plans that manage care through doctor networks (HMOs and similar plans). It would require plans to cover emergency care without prior approval under a 'prudent layperson' standard, let patients see specialists directly, guarantee an outside review when a plan denies care, ban contracts that stop doctors from telling patients about all treatment options, and let patients sue plans in state court for injuries. It applied to both employer and individual coverage and did not override stricter state laws.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans: patients who would no longer need advance approval for emergency room visits, patients with chronic illnesses who could see specialists directly, and enrollees denied care who would get faster appeals reviewed by a same-specialty doctor. Doctors also gain protections against gag clauses and arbitrary removal from networks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care patients and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency and urgent services 24/7 with no prior authorization whenever a prudent layperson would consider it an emergency, whether or not the provider is in the network.
Enrollees with chronic conditions or special needs get direct access to specialists, continuity of care when networks or employers change, and a point-of-service option to go outside the network.
Plans must run appeals reviewed by an independent clinical peer in the same specialty — within an hour for urgent care — and must not pay the reviewers who deny care.
Contract provisions that prohibit doctors from discussing their patient's health status, treatment options, or the plan's financial incentives are null and void.
Plans must disclose how premiums are split between care and administration, physician incentive arrangements that could limit services, and their denial-and-appeal track record.

State laws allowing lawsuits for personal injury or wrongful death against entities insuring or administering employer health plans are preserved, ending the ERISA shield that left injured patients with limited remedies.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs, which would bear compliance costs, disclosure obligations, new liability exposure in state courts, and restrictions on cost-control tools like prior authorization. Employers sponsoring group plans would face added administrative costs and possible litigation, which could feed into premiums. The bill explicitly did not require plans to accept every willing provider, preserving some network control.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies a long list of federal requirements to every health issuer and group plan — network adequacy demonstrations, point-of-service options, detailed disclosure of dozens of data points, utilization review timelines, credentialing committees, and quality programs — which insurers and employers argued would raise premiums and administrative costs for everyone, including people who did not want or need the extra coverage.

The state-liability provision (Section 4) would expose plans and their administrators to personal injury and wrongful death suits in state courts, which opponents said would drive up litigation costs and premiums rather than improve care.

Many of the standards defer to 'the applicable State authority' for definitions like access, undue burden, and urgent care, so the practical strength of protections would vary by state and depend on later regulation.

The bill preserves insurer discretion by explicitly rejecting an 'any willing provider' requirement, so plans could still exclude doctors from networks for economic reasons under objective published criteria.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address real, documented failures of 1990s managed care — surprise emergency bills, denial of specialist access, gag clauses, and patients unable to sue because federal ERISA law preempted state remedies. Those gains are substantial for the majority of insured Americans then in managed care. The honest costs are higher premiums from compliance and, especially, from the new right to sue; the bill's drafters tried to limit network disruption by keeping insurers' right to build their own networks. On balance the benefits to patients outweigh the cost concerns, though the liability provision was the most contested and expensive element.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees — Commerce and Education and the Workforce — was sent to subcommittees, got hearings in October 1997, and was never marked up or brought to the floor before Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Norwood, a Georgia Republican dentist, introduced the bill on April 23, 1997 with 65 original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to both the Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, then to the Health and Environment and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees in May 1997.
It drew 240 cosponsors — 96 Republicans, 143 Democrats, and 1 Independent — which, together with the sponsor, was a majority of the House.
The subcommittees held hearings on October 23 and 28, 1997, but the bill never received a markup or a vote in either full committee.
Norwood gave introductory remarks on the House floor on October 14, 1998, but no floor action ever followed; the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and HMOs were better off, because the bill died before its mandates and its removal of the federal ERISA liability shield could take effect, as did the large employers whose plans would have faced new state-court lawsuits and compliance costs. Patients gained nothing from this Congress; the broader patient-bill-of-rights fight continued in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, HMOs, and large employer plans

for.name: Rep. Charles Norwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 23, 1997, recruited 65 original cosponsors from both parties, and spoke on the House floor for it in October 1998.

for.name: 143 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, forming the largest share of its support.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership (Chairman Tom Bliley)
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Kept the bill in committee and its Health and Environment Subcommittee, where hearings were held in October 1997; the full committee never marked up or voted on the bill.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich and House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor despite a majority of the House sponsoring or cosponsoring it.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care (HMO) industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, particularly the provision stripping the federal ERISA shield that blocked state-court lawsuits over denied care, and lobbied against it.

against.name: Large employers and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the liability provision and new federal mandates on employer health plans, citing cost and litigation exposure.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 96 Republicans and 143 Democrats cosponsored — but the two committees that held the bill were chaired by Republicans, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would impose federal patient protections on all issuers and, through Section 4, would let patients sue them in state court for injuries, ending a key federal shield. Plans' interests in avoiding mandates and liability ran directly against patients' interest in enforceable rights.

Doctors gain a ban on gag clauses, due process for network participation and termination, an end to 'without cause' contract terminations, and protection from discrimination by license type. Their access to their patients' care decisions is strengthened, which serves patients too.

Employer plans would face compliance costs under ERISA Section 713 and new exposure to state personal-injury suits, costs that could be passed into premiums. But their employees would gain enforceable patient protections.
